check_service_status.description: Check whether the USGS earthquake catalog is answering, and how quickly. This is the one action that reports a problem as a value instead of failing the step, so a workflow can decide what to do about it - skip a digest, wait, or say the data is stale rather than dying halfway through. Being throttled is reported separately from being down.
check_service_status.display_str_template: Check the USGS earthquake catalog status.

mock_response.message: The USGS earthquake catalog is up, running API 2.8.4.

check_service_status.name: check_service_status

count_earthquakes.description: Count the earthquakes a search would match, without fetching any of them. One small answer however big the number, which makes it the cheap way for a schedule to ask 'was there anything?' before doing the expensive part - and the way to check a search is inside the 20,000 events one response can carry, since the catalog rejects a bigger one rather than trimming it.
count_earthquakes.name: count_earthquakes

parameters.description: Only events at or after this moment. Leave it and 'Days back' empty to use this action's own default window. Times are UTC unless the value says otherwise.
parameters.name: start_time

parameters.description: Only events at or before this moment. Leave it empty to search up to now, which is what a scheduled run almost always wants: the catalog decides what 'now' is, so an event that arrives while the step runs is still included.
parameters.name: end_time

parameters.description: Look this many days back instead of naming a start date - what a workflow that runs every morning needs, since 'the last 7 days' cannot be written as a fixed date. Counted back from now, or from 'End time' if you set one. Give this or 'Start time', not both.
parameters.name: days_back

parameters.description: Only events at or above this magnitude. This is the filter that decides how much noise a workflow sees: the catalog records tens of thousands of events a month, almost all of them too small to feel. 2.5 is roughly where people start noticing, 4.5 is the global reporting threshold, and 6 is where damage becomes likely.
parameters.name: min_magnitude

parameters.description: Only events at or below this magnitude.
parameters.name: max_magnitude

parameters.description: Only events at or below this depth, in kilometres. The catalog allows -100 to 1000; a negative depth is an event above sea level, which is normal in mountainous regions.
parameters.name: min_depth_km

parameters.description: Only events at or above this depth, in kilometres. Shallow events shake the surface far harder than deep ones of the same magnitude, so a filter of 70 km or less is a rough stand-in for 'the ones people felt'.
parameters.name: max_depth_km

parameters.description: The centre of a circle to search, in degrees from -90 to 90. Needs a longitude and a radius with it: given only part of a circle the catalog ignores the whole thing and returns events from everywhere, so a partial one is refused here instead.
parameters.name: latitude

parameters.description: The centre of a circle to search, in degrees from -180 to 180. Needs a latitude and a radius with it.
parameters.name: longitude

parameters.description: How far around the centre to look, in kilometres, up to 20,001.6 - which is half the Earth's circumference, and so the whole planet.
parameters.name: radius_km

parameters.description: The southern edge of a rectangle to search, -90 to 90. The four edges are independent: set only the two you care about to search a band of latitude or longitude.
parameters.name: min_latitude

parameters.description: The northern edge of a rectangle to search, -90 to 90.
parameters.name: max_latitude

parameters.description: The western edge of a rectangle to search. Normally -180 to 180, but the catalog lets a box cross the date line by going outside that: 170 to 190 is a real search over the western Pacific.
parameters.name: min_longitude

parameters.description: The eastern edge of a rectangle to search, -360 to 360.
parameters.name: max_longitude

parameters.description: Only events of this type. The catalog is not only earthquakes: it also records quarry blasts, explosions, mine collapses, sonic booms and ice quakes, and a search that names no type returns all of them. Choose 'earthquake' to leave the rest out.
parameters.name: event_type

parameters.description: Only events with a PAGER alert of at least this level, weakest first: green, yellow, orange, red. Worth knowing that this is really a 'has been assessed' filter - the USGS runs a PAGER loss assessment only on the events big enough to warrant one, so most events carry no alert at all and setting this to green still leaves out the great majority of them.
parameters.name: min_alert_level

parameters.description: Only events with at least this many 'Did You Feel It?' responses from the public. Like the alert level, this only ever matches events somebody reported, which is a small share of them - but it is the best single filter for 'an event people noticed' regardless of how big it measured.
parameters.name: min_felt_reports

parameters.description: Only events at or above this significance score. The catalog computes it from magnitude, felt reports and estimated impact together, so it ranks a moderate earthquake under a city above a large one in the deep ocean. Roughly: 600 and above is what makes the news, 1000 is a major disaster.
parameters.name: min_significance

parameters.description: Whether to include events a seismologist has not checked yet. Automatic solutions appear within minutes and are sometimes revised or withdrawn; reviewed ones are slower and settled. Defaults to all of them.
parameters.name: review_status

parameters.description: Only events from this catalog. Leave empty - the default - to get the most preferred information about each event from whichever catalog holds it, which is what almost every workflow wants.
parameters.name: catalog

parameters.description: Only events contributed by this network - 'ak' for Alaska, 'ci' for southern California, 'us' for the USGS national operation. Each event names its own in 'network'.
parameters.name: contributor

parameters.description: Only events that have this kind of product attached - a 'shakemap' for modelled shaking, 'dyfi' for public reports, 'losspager' for a casualty and loss estimate, 'moment-tensor' for the fault solution. A product is only generated when an event warrants it, so this doubles as a filter for the events the USGS itself treated as significant.
parameters.name: product_type

find_earthquakes_near_place.description: Find the earthquakes within a radius of a point - a site, an office, a customer's address - nearest first, each with how far away it was in kilometres and miles and which direction it lay. That distance is the thing a radius search leaves out: the catalog returns the events inside the circle but never says how far away any of them was, so it is worked out here. Defaults to a 100 km radius over the last 30 days.

get_aftershock_forecast.description: Get the USGS aftershock forecast for an earthquake: for the next day, week, month and year, the chance of at least one aftershock of each magnitude from 3 up and the range of how many to expect, with how many it has recorded so far and when the forecast will next be updated. The USGS forecasts after earthquakes of about magnitude 4 and up in the contiguous United States and 5 and up elsewhere in the US and its territories, and some others; for an event without one, 'available' comes back false rather than the step failing.

observed_aftershocks.description: How many aftershocks have been recorded so far at or above each magnitude.

For what the USGS has published about the event since, use Get an earthquake's impact, Get the aftershock forecast or Get an earthquake's fault mechanism.

Usually this comes from an earlier step rather than being typed: every action here returns the id of each event it hands back, and Get recent earthquakes or Search earthquakes is the normal way to get one. An id is a short code the reporting network assigns, such as 'nc75123456'.
parameters.name: event_id

get_earthquake_impact.description: Get what the USGS has assessed about an earthquake's effects, in one answer: its PAGER alert with the most likely range of deaths and of economic losses, the strongest shaking its ShakeMap models in plain words (such as 'Severe'), how many people reported feeling it, its landslide and liquefaction alerts, its tsunami flag, and links to the PAGER report and the shaking map. The USGS assesses earthquakes strong enough to be felt widely; for a small one 'assessed' comes back false rather than the step failing.

alert_level.description: The PAGER alert level: green, yellow, orange or red, the higher of the two below. Empty when PAGER has not assessed the event.

assessed.description: Whether the USGS has published any impact assessment (PAGER, ShakeMap, 'Did You Feel It?' or ground failure) for the event. False is normal for a small earthquake, and every field below is then empty.

economic_alert_level.description: PAGER's alert level for economic losses: green, yellow, orange or red.

event_id.description: The event id that was looked up.

fatality_alert_level.description: PAGER's alert level for deaths from shaking: green, yellow, orange or red.

felt_responses.description: How many people reported feeling it through 'Did You Feel It?'.

landslide_alert.description: The ground-failure model's landslide alert: green, yellow, orange or red.

liquefaction_alert.description: The ground-failure model's liquefaction alert: green, yellow, orange or red.

max_pga_g.description: The strongest ground acceleration on the ShakeMap, as a fraction of gravity (g).

available.description: Whether the USGS has published a moment tensor or focal mechanism for the event. When false, every field below is empty.

depth_km.description: The depth the solution puts the earthquake at, in kilometres.

event_id.description: The event id that was looked up.

faulting_style.description: The kind of faulting, read from the first plane's rake: strike-slip (the sides slid past each other), reverse (one side pushed up over the other), normal (one side dropped down), oblique-reverse or oblique-normal.

message.description: The faulting in one line, ready for a message, or why there is none.

moment_magnitude.description: The magnitude the moment tensor gives. Empty for a focal mechanism.

moment_magnitude_type.description: The kind of moment magnitude, such as 'Mww'.

nodal_plane_1.description: One of the two planes the fault could lie on. The solution alone cannot tell which is the real fault and which its mirror.

dip.description: How steeply the plane slopes down from horizontal, in degrees (90 is vertical).

rake.description: The direction of slip within the plane, in degrees: about 0 or 180 is sideways, 90 is one side pushed up, -90 is one side dropping down.

strike.description: The plane's compass direction along the ground, in degrees clockwise from north.

dip.description: How steeply the plane slopes down from horizontal, in degrees (90 is vertical).

rake.description: The direction of slip within the plane, in degrees: about 0 or 180 is sideways, 90 is one side pushed up, -90 is one side dropping down.

strike.description: The plane's compass direction along the ground, in degrees clockwise from north.

percent_double_couple.description: How much of the motion a single fault explains, in percent. Near 100 is a clean single-fault rupture.

review_status.description: Whether a seismologist has reviewed the solution: 'reviewed' or 'automatic'.

scalar_moment_nm.description: The size of the slip as a seismic moment, in newton-metres.

solution_count.description: How many moment tensors and focal mechanisms have been published for the event, of which this is the preferred one.

solution_type.description: Where the answer comes from: 'moment tensor' or 'focal mechanism'.

source.description: The network that published the solution, such as 'us'.

get_largest_earthquake.description: Find the single biggest earthquake in a window, optionally within a region - the one line a weekly digest or a morning briefing wants. A quiet window is reported as 'found: false' with a message rather than as a failure, so a scheduled post can say 'nothing above M4 this week' instead of the step dying on the weeks when that is the news. Defaults to the last 7 days.

parameters.description: Which feed to read. The USGS publishes one per magnitude floor: 'significant' is the handful it has judged newsworthy, then 4.5+, 2.5+, 1.0+, and 'all', which is every event it recorded and can run to tens of thousands in a month. parameters.description: How far back the feed covers. Match it to how often the workflow runs, with room to spare: an hourly schedule reading the past-day feed never misses an event because one run was late.

parameters.description: How far around the centre to look, in kilometres, up to 20,001.6 - which is half the Earth's circumference, and so the whole planet.
parameters.name: radius_km

parameters.description: The southern edge of a rectangle to search, -90 to 90. The four edges are independent: set only the two you care about to search a band of latitude or longitude.
parameters.name: min_latitude

parameters.description: The northern edge of a rectangle to search, -90 to 90.
parameters.name: max_latitude

parameters.description: The western edge of a rectangle to search. Normally -180 to 180, but the catalog lets a box cross the date line by going outside that: 170 to 190 is a real search over the western Pacific.
parameters.name: min_longitude

parameters.description: The eastern edge of a rectangle to search, -360 to 360.
parameters.name: max_longitude

parameters.description: Only events of this type. The catalog is not only earthquakes: it also records quarry blasts, explosions, mine collapses, sonic booms and ice quakes, and a search that names no type returns all of them. Choose 'earthquake' to leave the rest out.
parameters.name: event_type

parameters.description: Only events with a PAGER alert of at least this level, weakest first: green, yellow, orange, red. Worth knowing that this is really a 'has been assessed' filter - the USGS runs a PAGER loss assessment only on the events big enough to warrant one, so most events carry no alert at all and setting this to green still leaves out the great majority of them.
parameters.name: min_alert_level

parameters.description: Only events with at least this many 'Did You Feel It?' responses from the public. Like the alert level, this only ever matches events somebody reported, which is a small share of them - but it is the best single filter for 'an event people noticed' regardless of how big it measured.
parameters.name: min_felt_reports

parameters.description: Only events at or above this significance score. The catalog computes it from magnitude, felt reports and estimated impact together, so it ranks a moderate earthquake under a city above a large one in the deep ocean. Roughly: 600 and above is what makes the news, 1000 is a major disaster.
parameters.name: min_significance

parameters.description: Whether to include events a seismologist has not checked yet. Automatic solutions appear within minutes and are sometimes revised or withdrawn; reviewed ones are slower and settled. Defaults to all of them.
parameters.name: review_status

parameters.description: Only events from this catalog. Leave empty - the default - to get the most preferred information about each event from whichever catalog holds it, which is what almost every workflow wants.
parameters.name: catalog

parameters.description: Only events contributed by this network - 'ak' for Alaska, 'ci' for southern California, 'us' for the USGS national operation. Each event names its own in 'network'.
parameters.name: contributor

parameters.description: Only events that have this kind of product attached - a 'shakemap' for modelled shaking, 'dyfi' for public reports, 'losspager' for a casualty and loss estimate, 'moment-tensor' for the fault solution. A product is only generated when an event warrants it, so this doubles as a filter for the events the USGS itself treated as significant.
parameters.name: product_type

parameters.description: Only events whose record changed after this moment, whenever the earthquake itself happened. This is how a workflow keeps a copy in step: a solution revised days later shows up here even though its time has not moved.
parameters.name: updated_after

parameters.description: Whether to include events the catalog has deleted, which it does when review shows an event was not real or was a duplicate. Left out by default. A workflow keeping its own copy in step with 'Updated after' needs them, or a withdrawn event simply stops appearing and the copy never drops it; a deleted event comes back with its status set to 'deleted'.
parameters.name: include_deleted

parameters.description: How the catalog should order the results.
parameters.name: order_by

parameters.description: How many events to return, from 1 to 20,000. Defaults to 50. The catalog rejects a search whose result would run past 20,000 rather than trimming it, so run Count earthquakes first if a window might be that busy.
parameters.name: limit

parameters.description: Skip to this position in the results, counting from 1, to page through a search bigger than one call. Pair it with the same ordering every time, or two pages can overlap.
parameters.name: offset

summarize_earthquakes.description: Summarise a window's seismic activity for a digest: how many events, how they split across the magnitude bands, the largest and the most significant, how many people felt, how many carried a tsunami flag, and the regions with the most activity. The total is exact however busy the window; the rest is computed over the events read, and 'complete' says whether those are the same set. Defaults to the last 7 days.

largest.title: M 6.1 - 95 km SSW of Sand Point, Alaska

most_significant.place: 95 km SSW of Sand Point, Alaska
most_significant.title: M 6.1 - 95 km SSW of Sand Point, Alaska

summarize_earthquakes.name: summarize_earthquakes

parameters.description: Only events at or after this moment. Leave it and 'Days back' empty to use this action's own default window. Times are UTC unless the value says otherwise.
parameters.name: start_time

parameters.description: Only events at or before this moment. Leave it empty to search up to now, which is what a scheduled run almost always wants: the catalog decides what 'now' is, so an event that arrives while the step runs is still included.
parameters.name: end_time

parameters.description: Look this many days back instead of naming a start date - what a workflow that runs every morning needs, since 'the last 7 days' cannot be written as a fixed date. Counted back from now, or from 'End time' if you set one. Give this or 'Start time', not both.
parameters.name: days_back

parameters.description: Only events at or above this magnitude. This is the filter that decides how much noise a workflow sees: the catalog records tens of thousands of events a month, almost all of them too small to feel. 2.5 is roughly where people start noticing, 4.5 is the global reporting threshold, and 6 is where damage becomes likely.
parameters.name: min_magnitude

parameters.description: The centre of a circle to search, in degrees from -90 to 90. Needs a longitude and a radius with it: given only part of a circle the catalog ignores the whole thing and returns events from everywhere, so a partial one is refused here instead.
parameters.name: latitude

parameters.name: event_type

parameters.description: How many events to read for the figures, from 1 to 20,000. Defaults to 1,000, which covers a normal week above magnitude 2.5 several times over. Raise it for a wider window or a lower magnitude floor; the total is counted separately and stays exact either way.
parameters.name: sample_limit

description: Read the USGS Earthquake Catalog: every earthquake the USGS and its contributing networks have recorded, from this minute back through the last century. Watch the real-time feeds on a schedule, search the catalog by time, magnitude, depth, region or PAGER alert level, geo-fence a site and see how far away each event was and in which direction, count a window before you fetch it, pull the largest event of the week, or summarise a period for a digest. After a large one, get the USGS's assessment of its impact (PAGER alert, likely deaths and losses, strongest shaking), the aftershock forecast and how the fault moved. No API key, no sign-up and no quota.
